frame: I operate an AI-native development environment where specialized agents handle much of the implementation execution. I own requirements, architecture, orchestration, evaluation, deployment, monitoring and production decisions.

entries.q: Who writes the code?
entries.a: Specialized AI agents do much of the implementation. I own what gets built, what gets accepted, what gets deployed and what happens when it breaks: I write the requirements, decide the tests a change must pass, and accept it only when the tests and the production logs prove it works.
entries.push: Could you do it without AI? — Not at this speed, and that is the point: the job is outcomes, and my AI environment is how I deliver them.

entries.q: How do you evaluate an AI system before it ships?
entries.a: Two layers. Automated tests check every rule on every change — hundreds of them, in about a minute. Then an offline replay re-runs the model on real past decisions, each stored with the posting it was made on. If a change scores worse, it does not ship: a RAG upgrade stayed switched off for exactly that reason.
entries.push: Why did RAG score worse? — Label noise: near-identical past jobs had opposite decisions, so the retrieved examples pulled the model both ways.

entries.q: What does the model decide, and what does code decide?
entries.a: Hard facts stated in the input go in code: a country restriction, a pay figure, 'no AI tools'. Judgment calls go to the model. When they disagree, the code checks the source facts, never the model's stated reason — models sometimes give the right verdict with the wrong reason.
entries.push: An example? — An override of mine once released three correct rejections because it saw the word 'LATAM' and ignored 'U.S. only'. Now it asks the same location checker the filters use.

entries.q: What does fail-closed mean in your systems?
entries.a: When something is wrong, the system refuses instead of guessing. My outreach sends only after one human click and refuses the whole send if an attachment fails to load; my publisher will not print a number it cannot trace to a source.
entries.push: Isn't that bad for throughput? — Sometimes it costs one send. A wrong attachment in front of a client costs trust, so I choose per workflow which failure is cheaper.

entries.q: What happens when your LLM provider fails?
entries.a: Nothing breaks. Every model call has an ordered fallback across five providers — Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Grok and Groq. My Anthropic balance has been at zero for weeks and the systems keep running on the next provider; when Groq retired the models I used, it was a config change, not an outage.
entries.push: How do you know it works? — A test deliberately loses the first providers and checks the chain still answers, and the logs name which provider served each call.

entries.q: How do you implement agent memory?
entries.a: Three kinds: a permanent ledger of decisions for learning; semantic memory — my tutor bot stores conversation turns as embeddings in Postgres with pgvector and retrieves the three most similar before replying (497 memories, no retrieval errors in the last week); and a short session memory, so 'change it' edits the item just created.
entries.push: The risks? — Stale or wrong memories. So memory is scoped per user, has a similarity threshold, and fails safe: no memory rather than a crash.

entries.q: How do you find a bottleneck?
entries.a: I check the output, not whether the process ran. One of my search paths ran on schedule with its filters silently switched off: a library failed to load and the error went to a log level production never prints. I found it by loading the process exactly as production does; the first fixed run rejected five junk results that used to become CRM deals.
entries.push: The lesson? — 'It ran' is not 'it worked': prove every change produced the right output.

entries.q: How do you measure impact?
entries.a: I pick the number that tracks money or time, measure it before and after, and keep only changes that move it. A new job source cleared my live filter 72% of the time, measured across all 345 of its postings, so it stayed. I also fix the measurement itself: my replay was scoring on blank postings until I stored the real one behind each decision.

entries.q: Tell me about an incident you handled.
entries.a: My server hit 95% disk because no log had ever been trimmed. I compressed 8.5 GB of logs to 310 MB — removing each original only after checking the copy byte for byte — kept every service running, capped the system journal after a full backup, and set up rotation so it cannot recur.
entries.push: The named concept? — A retention policy. On the way I found a library writing a bot token into logs thousands of times a day and silenced it at the source: secrets in logs.

entries.q: How do you handle client delivery and SLAs?
entries.a: I haven't run US-client SLAs yet. I ran delivery at board level for seven years in regulated e-government: vendor coordination, operational delivery, cost and performance reporting. My own systems work the same way: define what 'working' means, measure it from production logs, and get alerted before the client notices.
entries.push: A client says the AI is wrong? — Reproduce it on their real case, find whether it is the data, the rules or the model, fix the cheapest layer, add a test so it stays fixed, and tell them what changed.

entries.q: How would you grow an account?
entries.a: Deliver one measurable win in their main bottleneck, show the number, then propose the next bottleneck with a cost and an expected result. As Deputy CEO for business development at a fintech, and in my own outreach loop, I learned clients buy outcomes, not models.

entries.q: What is MCP, and how do you use it?
entries.a: The Model Context Protocol is a standard way to give an AI agent tools — a CRM, a search engine, a browser. My agents use MCP connectors in my development environment every day; in production my systems call the HubSpot, Resend, Telegram and Trello APIs directly, with code guards on what the model may decide.
entries.push: The risks? — An agent with tools can act, so anything irreversible or outward-facing needs a human approval step.

entries.q: Walk me through your CRM automation.
entries.a: My acquisition loop runs in production: research, qualify, draft, one human tap, send, then delivery and opens written back to HubSpot — 800+ business prospects so far. Every writer tags its deals with a source prefix, and a daily read-back audit re-reads HubSpot to prove the notes and attachments really landed.
entries.push: Why read back? — Because 'the API said OK' is not proof: reconciliation checks the result, not the request.

entries.q: What is GEO/AEO, and how do you measure it?
entries.a: Generative and answer-engine optimization: making a company visible and quotable in ChatGPT, Perplexity and Claude, not only Google. My public AI Visibility Audit API scores a site with 34 automated checks; in the server logs for 1–10 October alone it ran 39 audits of 18 websites, 18 of them by people on the public page.
entries.push: How is it different from SEO? — The same foundations (crawlability, structured data), plus access for AI crawlers and content an answer engine can quote.

entries.q: How do you decide what to build?
entries.a: Bottleneck first: find where money or time is lost, ship the smallest change that tests the fix, measure it, then harden what works. My acceptance criteria are tests a change must pass, and a feature that measures worse does not ship — even a technically impressive one.

entries.q: How do you work under regulation?
entries.a: Seven years as Deputy CEO and Chief Legal Officer in regulated e-government taught me to treat constraints as product inputs. In my AI systems that means hard rules in code, fail-closed defaults, a human approval before anything irreversible, and no number shown unless it traces back to a record.

entries.q: How do you produce a film with AI?
entries.a: Through a pipeline I built: poems from my own ATUONA universe become shots generated per type after a model bake-off; narration is locked to each clip and the mix is normalised to broadcast loudness; every render is checked before release. Eight films are published; the latest, Crimson Escape, runs 3:36 from 16 shots.

entries.q: You don't have an engineering degree — why you?
entries.a: Because the role is outcomes, not a degree: I find the real bottleneck, get the system built and measured, and explain it to the client. My degree isn't in engineering; since May 2025 I have built and run 15 production services through my AI environment.

entries.q: How do you handle hallucination risk?
entries.a: As a production incident, not a prompt problem. My daily publisher once fell to a cheaper fallback model when a provider balance ran out, and for ten weeks it described a database the system has never used while every run reported clean. I stopped it at the source and rebuilt it to write only from a bundle of facts measured on the running system: an article with a number absent from that bundle, or naming infrastructure that is not installed, is rejected and regenerated, and a day with too few verified facts gets no article. Three days later the gate refused a number that had leaked in from the topic prompt itself, so the prompt is now treated as a source too: every number in it is licensed or stripped.
entries.push: How do you know the gate works? — It fired in production on 26 August: the run was skipped with 'Grounding gate / unsourced number(s): 40', and the day's article shipped once the brief was cleaned. The named lesson: redundancy protects availability, not truth — a provider downgrade is an editorial event, not only an operational one.

entries.q: How do you control vendor and LLM cost?
entries.a: Hard caps in code, checked against the vendor's real response, and fallbacks that keep service up when a balance runs out. I found a spending cap that could never fire: the budget guard read a price field the vendor never sends, so every price passed. I fixed it against the vendor's actual response and published the postmortem. When a provider's balance ran out, the five-provider fallback chain kept the bots answering, and the same event taught me that a fallback can also change what the model says, so cost events are watched for quality, not only for availability.
entries.push: Do you track LLM token spend and latency? — Not as a telemetry stack yet. I track vendor spend per run against a cap and watch balances; token-level and latency telemetry is what I would set up first for a client budget.

entries.q: How do you align stakeholders and compliance?
entries.a: Seven years as Deputy CEO and Chief Legal Officer of a regional e-government operator: I owned the board process for stakeholders drawn mainly from the regional government, drove its decisions through to implementation, and made sure every public service we moved online was lawful under existing legislation. That taught me to treat constraints as product inputs. In my AI systems it means hard rules in code, fail-closed defaults, a human approval before anything irreversible, and no number shown unless it traces back to a record.
entries.push: Have you done it with a U.S. enterprise client? — Not yet. I ran delivery at board level for seven years in regulated e-government: vendor coordination, operational delivery, cost and performance reporting; the client-facing part of this role is where I would lean on that.
